sm: The host, Roman Balmakov, reports that the Pentagon has allowed the Department of Homeland Security to borrow a military heat-ray weapon for use at the southern border. The military says the invisible beam reaches people more than half a mile away and causes a burning sensation on the skin for ten to fifteen minutes, similar to opening a hot oven door, which makes people instinctively run. He traces the history of the Active Denial System: the Air Force began studying millimeter wave energy in the late 1980s, found that waves near 95 gigahertz rapidly heat the skin's surface, and demonstrated a first shipping-container-sized system in December 2000. A smaller version was later mounted on a Humvee. The military has let reporters try it, including an Associated Press reporter in 2007 and a 60 Minutes reporter, who described it as scalding water, and Marines held a public demonstration at Quantico in 2012.

Balmakov says safety has been the main concern, and the military has spent twenty years on lab and human testing covering skin injuries, eye exposure, reproductive effects and cancer risk. Studies found a wide margin between feeling the heat and being burned, the eye blinks within a quarter second, and a 2001 animal study found no significant increase in tumors. A 2009 National Defense University report cited over 11,000 exposures of more than 700 people, with eight second-degree burns, and in 2025 the Department of War said the system had been tested over 15,000 times with under a tenth of one percent chance of injury. He recounts an April 2007 incident at Moody Air Force Base where an airman was burned because settings of 100 percent power for four seconds were never reset after a long-distance test. The airman left the hospital after two days and returned to work two weeks later. Finally, a memo signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth authorizes a seven-month loan of one system starting in September, not to be operated by Pentagon personnel, with Homeland Security solely responsible for its use and for developing tactics.
